blocks.content: An inode, short for index node, is the concrete data structure Unix and Linux style file systems use to hold everything about a file except its name. Understanding inodes precisely explains two things that otherwise seem like magic: why a hard link keeps working after the original name is deleted, and how a file system supports files far larger than any single fixed size structure could describe on its own.

This chapter builds on the directory structure chapter's central insight, that a directory is a table mapping names to references, by looking closely at exactly what those references point to, and what a file system actually does with them.
1. What an Inode Actually Is

An inode is a fixed size data structure, one per file, stored in a reserved area of the disk, that holds all of a file's metadata together with the pointers needed to locate its actual data blocks. Every regular file, every directory, and every symbolic link on the file system has exactly one inode describing it.

The detail that surprises people the first time they see it is what an inode does not store: the file's name. Naming is handled entirely by directory entries, a directory entry pairs a name with an inode number, and the inode itself has no idea what name or names currently point at it. This separation between naming and everything else is the single most important idea in this whole chapter.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195023-170699197.png

blocks.title: The one insight to keep
blocks.content: A file's name lives only in a directory entry. Its inode holds the metadata and the data block pointers, and has no concept of what it is currently called.
2. What an Inode Actually Contains
Beyond the frame or block pointers, a typical inode packs in a specific, well defined set of fields, each one answering a question the file system needs to answer quickly and often.

{"headers":["Field","What it holds"],"rows":[["File type","Whether this inode describes a regular file, a directory, or a symbolic link"],["Size","The file's length in bytes"],["Owner","The user and group ID that own the file, used for permission checks"],["Permission bits","Read, write, execute permissions for owner, group, and everyone else"],["Timestamps","Typically three distinct ones: last accessed, last modified, and last inode change"],["Link count","How many directory entries currently point at this inode"],["Data block pointers","Where on disk the file's actual content physically lives"]]}

3. The Inode Number

Every inode has a unique number within its file system, and this number is exactly what a directory entry stores as its reference, not a raw disk address, not a pointer in the programming language sense, just a plain integer that the file system knows how to look up.

This means a directory entry is really just a name paired with an inode number, nothing more. Looking up a file by path means walking through directory tables, following inode numbers, until the final inode is reached.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195023-548783147.png
4. Why Hard Links Work: The Link Count
blocks.text: 4. Why Hard Links Work: The Link Count

blocks.content: This is where the name versus inode separation pays off directly. A hard link, covered in the directory structure chapter, is simply a new directory entry, a new name, that points at an existing, already used inode number, not a new inode at all.

Every inode tracks exactly how many directory entries currently point at it, in its link count field. Creating a file starts that count at 1. Adding a hard link increments it. Deleting any one of the names pointing at that inode decrements it. Crucially, the file system only actually frees the inode and its data blocks once the link count drops all the way to 0, meaning no name anywhere still refers to it.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195023-505574238.png
blocks.alt: Why Hard Links Work: The Link Count

blocks.content: A worked numeric example

["Create a.txt. A fresh inode 118 is allocated, link count starts at 1.","Create a hard link b.txt pointing at the same inode 118. Link count increases to 2.","Delete the original name a.txt. Link count drops to 1, but the data is still fully intact and fully accessible through b.txt.","Only once b.txt is also deleted, dropping the link count to 0, does the file system actually reclaim inode 118 and its data blocks."]
items: Create a.txt. A fresh inode 118 is allocated, link count starts at 1.
Create a hard link b.txt pointing at the same inode 118. Link count increases to 2.
Delete the original name a.txt. Link count drops to 1, but the data is still fully intact and fully accessible through b.txt.
Only once b.txt is also deleted, dropping the link count to 0, does the file system actually reclaim inode 118 and its data blocks.

blocks.content: 5. Direct, Indirect, and Double Indirect Pointers
blocks.text: 5. Direct, Indirect, and Double Indirect Pointers

blocks.content: An inode is fixed size, but files obviously are not, some are a few bytes, others are many gigabytes. The classic mechanism for handling both extremes efficiently, without making every inode enormous just to accommodate rare huge files, is a layered system of direct and indirect pointers.

A fixed number of direct pointers live inside the inode itself and point straight at data blocks, fast, no extra lookup, ideal for small files that fit entirely within them. Once a file outgrows what the direct pointers can address, the inode falls back to an indirect pointer, which does not point at data at all, it points at an entire separate block that is itself completely full of more pointers to actual data blocks.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195023-93616260.png
blocks.alt: Direct, Indirect, and Double Indirect Pointers

blocks.content: For truly enormous files, a double indirect pointer goes one layer further: it points at a block full of indirect pointers, each of which points at its own block full of direct data pointers. This layered structure keeps the inode itself small and fixed size while still scaling up to handle files many orders of magnitude larger than the direct pointers alone could ever reach.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195024-648333335.png
blocks.alt: Direct, Indirect, and Double Indirect Pointers

blocks.content: 6. A Worked Example with Real Numbers
blocks.text: 6. A Worked Example with Real Numbers

blocks.content: Concrete numbers make the size scaling clear. Assume 12 direct pointers inside the inode, each addressing a 4KB block, and assume each indirect block can itself hold 1024 pointers.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195653-69795566.png
blocks.alt: A Worked Example with Real Numbers

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pointer layer","How it addresses data","Roughly how much size it adds"],"rows":[["12 direct pointers","Straight to 12 individual 4KB blocks","About 48KB, directly from the inode"],["1 single indirect pointer","To a block of 1024 pointers, each to a 4KB block","About 4MB more, beyond the direct range"],["1 double indirect pointer","To a block of 1024 indirect pointers, each addressing about 4MB","About 4GB more, beyond the single indirect range"]]}

A tiny file only ever touches the first few direct pointers and pays no extra cost at all. A file that grows into the megabytes or gigabytes range gracefully falls through to the indirect layers, at the modest cost of one extra disk read to fetch the indirect pointer block itself before the actual data can be reached.
7. Inverted Page Tables: A Related Alternative Idea
blocks.text: 7. Inverted Page Tables: A Related Alternative Idea

blocks.content: A related design worth knowing, used for memory page tables rather than file inodes but built on the exact same indexing insight, is the inverted structure. Instead of one full mapping table per process, indexed by that process own page number, an inverted table flips the indexing entirely: one single shared table, indexed by physical frame number, records which process and which page currently occupies each frame.

This keeps total table size proportional to how much physical memory or disk exists, not to how many processes or files are active, exactly the same kind of space saving spirit that indexed and multilevel inode pointers bring to file storage, just applied to a different resource.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195653-529563570.png
blocks.alt: Inverted Page Tables: A Related Alternative Idea

blocks.content: 8. Deleting a File: What Actually Happens
blocks.text: 8. Deleting a File: What Actually Happens

blocks.content: Running a delete command on a file's last remaining name does not necessarily free its disk space the instant the command returns. What actually happens is that the link count on its inode is decremented and the directory entry is removed. The underlying data blocks and the inode itself are only truly freed once that link count reaches zero and no running process still has the file open through an existing file descriptor.

This second condition matters in practice more than people expect: a process that opened a file and then had its last directory entry deleted by something else can keep reading and writing it perfectly normally, since the inode and its data blocks remain allocated as long as that open handle exists, only actually vanishing once the process closes it.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409195654-253956657.png
blocks.alt: Deleting a File: What Actually Happens

blocks.title: A common surprise
blocks.content: A running program can keep writing to a file that has already been deleted from every directory. The inode and data blocks stay alive as long as any process still holds it open, and are only reclaimed once the very last reference, whether a directory entry or an open handle, disappears.
9. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Assuming a file's name is stored somewhere inside its own inode, when it is not, the name only ever exists in directory entries pointing at the inode.","Underestimating how much space a single flat, non layered structure would require at real file sizes, which is exactly why the direct plus indirect plus double indirect layering exists in the first place.","Assuming deleting a file's last name always instantly frees its disk space, when the link count and any still open process handles both matter first."]
items: Assuming a file's name is stored somewhere inside its own inode, when it is not, the name only ever exists in directory entries pointing at the inode.

Underestimating how much space a single flat, non layered structure would require at real file sizes, which is exactly why the direct plus indirect plus double indirect layering exists in the first place.
Assuming deleting a file's last name always instantly frees its disk space, when the link count and any still open process handles both matter first.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain precisely why a hard link does not break when the original name is deleted, using the inode and link count mechanism from section 4, a very common systems interview question, and one that most wrong answers get backwards by assuming the data disappears with the first name.

The inode is the quiet workhorse behind almost every Unix and Linux file operation covered elsewhere in this module, hard links, file allocation via its pointer structure, even how deletion actually behaves, all trace back to this one fixed size structure and its link count.
